name: Opus 5 vol regime
strategy: Classified the current tape as a calm-index / high-dispersion regime (SPY 20d realized vol 11.65%, 34th percentile of two years, 10d/60d term ratio 0.80, versus QQQ 23.66% and XLK 30.67% at the ~80th percentile, and an implied-correlation proxy that has fallen from 0.54 to 0.34), and sized the book to that state: 60% in vol-targeted low-vol equity (USMV, SPLV) rather than the high-vol tech complex, 12% in SVXY to harvest the ~7-point gap between VIX 18.6 and SPY realized 11.65, a delta-neutral short-gamma pair of equal short TQQQ and short SQQQ to collect leveraged-ETF compounding decay, and 5% VIXY as convex crash insurance with a take-profit that monetises a spike.

positions.thesis: The new core, and the point of the whole rebalance. Cboe implied correlation is at its lowest in at least 23 years - COR3M ~9-10 against a 52-week range of 9.29-11.95, COR1M printing 8.7-9.93, expected average single-stock correlation ~23%. Index variance is approximately average constituent variance times correlation, so at these readings the S&P realizes 13.49% (20d, close-to-close) while its average member realizes far more. That is diversification benefit at a two-decade maximum, and it is free. Every other way I have owned equity in this book paid for its low volatility: USMV pays in surrendered expected return (+5.21% YTD vs SPLV's +9.98% and an index at record highs), SPLV pays by concentrating 25.4% in utilities. SPY pays nothing for it. In a genuinely high-dispersion regime the correct long-only expression is to own the index rather than its components, because dispersion is exactly what makes the wrapper safer than its contents - and I had been drawing the opposite conclusion from the same data, buying low-vol stocks when the dispersion I identified was an argument for the index. Sized at 40% rather than higher for two reasons: the melt-up ran on a jobs contraction, which is the rate channel doing the work rather than earnings, and the 15-16 Sep FOMC still carries a 44%-priced hike under Warsh. The -18% stop is deliberately wide - it is a regime-break brake, not a trading stop, because VIXY is the actual hedge and stacking a tight stop on top of a convex hedge is double-paying for the same protection and inviting a whipsaw out of the position at the worst moment.

Cut from 46% to 22% but kept, because the evidence I gathered for it is still good and only its role changed. What survives: MSCI's min-vol optimizer explicitly excludes high-volatility constituents, so the 31.82% technology label sits in low-beta software, services and payments rather than semiconductors - demonstrated on 29-Jul when USMV fell 0.21% against SMH -4.79% and SPY -1.54%, a ~14% downside capture no fund with real semi exposure could post. 20d realized 9.97%, issuer 3yr beta 0.49, 6.96% utilities so the least rate-sensitive of my defensive sleeves with the 10y at ~4.68%. What no longer holds: that this deserves to be the single largest line. It is +5.21% YTD against an index at a record high, and the low volatility is bought with foregone return, whereas SPY's is bought with correlation that is at a 23-year low and therefore unusually generous. So USMV moves from being the thesis to being ballast - the sleeve that keeps working if a soft-landing rotation punishes beta without a volatility event, which is the one state where neither SPY nor VIXY helps me. The -14% stop is unchanged and now caps this leg near -3.1% of NAV rather than -6.4%.

Cut hardest, from 32% to 12%, because it is the leg whose bull case is most dependent on a rate path the calendar may not deliver. The reason to own it is unchanged and still real: 1.78% technology against USMV's 31.82% makes it the only genuinely tech-free sleeve I have, and it fails in different states than USMV, which is why owning a little of both is actual diversification rather than duplication. But ~25.4% utilities is a direct short-rates position, and the Fed under Warsh held in July with hawkish dissents pushing to tighten and still carries a ~44% market-implied probability of a hike on 15-16 Sep even after a -23k payroll print. SPLV's +9.98% YTD lead over USMV was earned in a window where that risk was not being priced, and it now trades within ~1% of its 52-week high, which is where the crowded defensive trade lives. I am not willing to keep a third of the book in a single rate expression I cannot hedge, so I keep the diversification and shed the concentration. The stop stays wide at -16% for the original reason: ordinary rate noise in the utility sleeve must not knock me out of a position I hold specifically for its tech-free composition.

Upsized from 6% to 11% because every input that sets the price of this hedge improved at once. Level: VIX closed 15.15, the lowest print of this experiment and ~9% below where I last added. Value against realized: SPY 20d realized is 13.49%, so the risk premium I am paying is ~1.7 points against a ~3-4 point historical norm - insurance is close to fair on realized alone, which almost never happens. Carry: the curve is in compressed contango at VX6/VX1 1.062 versus a 1.15-1.20 historical average, so the roll cost is a third to a half of the ~43.8%/yr I underwrote at entry, and my single largest objection to this leg has weakened materially. And the free option: Cboe implied correlation at a 23-year low of ~9-10 means index vol is being suppressed by dispersion rather than by calm, so I get paid if realized vol rises OR if correlation simply reverts, and correlation at the bottom of a 23-year range can essentially only revert upward. Against that, three dated binaries inside the horizon: CPI on 12-Aug with energy still +15.7% y/y, a Hormuz negotiation that stalled Friday over a 5-7% vs 3% vs zero transit-fee dispute with Brent at $80, and a 15-16 Sep FOMC with a live hike at 44%. This is what makes the 40% SPY line affordable - convexity bought cheaply is a permission to carry beta, not a substitute for it, and last week I paid for the insurance without using the permission. Take-profit widened from +50% to +60%: off a VIX-15 base a +50% move now corresponds to a smaller absolute dislocation than it did at VIX 20, and I want this to survive a moderate scare intact and only convert to cash on a genuine one. No stop, for the same reason as always - stopping out of insurance while it is losing money is the single thing insurance must never do.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two things moved enough to force this, and they point the same way. First, the volatility risk premium has closed: VIX 15.15 against SPY 20d realized 13.49% is ~1.7 points, versus a ~3-4 point norm, so index vol is no longer expensive - and Cboe implied correlation sits at a 23-year low (COR3M ~9-10, 52-week range 9.29-11.95), which is a bounded, mean-reverting quantity that can only normalise upward. Long index vol therefore pays if realized rises OR correlation normalises, and the compressed contango (VX6/VX1 1.062 vs a 1.15-1.20 norm) means I pay a third-to-half the carry I underwrote at entry. Cheaper insurance against a denser calendar - CPI 12-Aug, a stalled Hormuz fee dispute with Brent at $80, and a 15-16 Sep FOMC where a Warsh hike is still 44% priced after payrolls printed -23k with 103k of downward revisions. Second, and this is the correction I owe myself: I have been conflating vol targeting with owning low-vol stocks. Vol targeting scales exposure to the INDEX by the index's realized vol. USMV and SPLV buy their low vol by surrendering expected return and by parking 25% of SPLV in utilities ahead of a live hike; the index buys its low vol from diversification, which is free and is at a 23-year maximum precisely because correlation is at a 23-year low. At COR3M ~10 the S&P realizes 13.5% while its average constituent realizes far more - that makes SPY the cheapest carrier of equity risk in my universe right now, not USMV. My book was carrying only ~40 SPY-equivalent betas into a low-correlation, low-index-vol tape and made +0.97% while the index made +3.58% and tech made +7.2%. The fix is not to abandon defence, it is to take the permission the insurance already bought: raise index beta and raise the hedge together. Modelled across three states - calm melt-up, moderate scare, and a VIX-doubling shock - the new shape beats the old one in every one, because more cheap convexity is what makes more beta affordable rather than a substitute for it.
novelty: This book is a low-correlation index-carry expression - long the S&P itself as the diversification-cheapest vehicle for equity risk while implied correlation sits at a 23-year low, financed against an upsized long-index-volatility leg bought at a 1.7-point risk premium with compressed contango; the low-vol factor sleeve is demoted from the core to residual ballast rather than being the thesis, which inverts the construction I ran for the prior three weeks.
research_notes:
WEEK IN REVIEW (2026-08-03 to 08-07). The tape went vertical: S&P 500 +3.58% to a record 7,757.64, Nasdaq +5.19%, Dow +2.96% through 54,000, Technology sector +7.2% and Materials +4.8%. My book made +0.97%. That gap is the finding, not the noise.

WHY IT RALLIED. July payrolls printed -23,000 against ~+80,000 expected, with May revised 129k->63k and June 57k->20k (-103k combined) and participation at 61.4%, a five-year low. Unemployment 4.1%. AHE +3.2% y/y vs +3.5% expected. Equities rallied on this because Warsh's Fed had a live HIKE on the table for 15-16 Sep (July hold at 3.50-3.75% carried hawkish dissents); the soft print cut hike odds from 57% to 44%. A market that makes an all-time high on a contracting labour market, purely through the rate channel, has inverted its good-news/bad-news polarity. 44% is still a coin flip on a hike.

VOL STATE. VIX closed 15.15 (-4.2% on the day), the lowest reading in this experiment. SPY 20d close-to-close realized was 13.49% at 31-Jul; SPY IV rank 12.49 at 03-Aug. So the volatility risk premium is roughly 15.15 - 13.5 = ~1.7 points, versus the ~7 points I sized the (now closed) SVXY leg against and a ~3-4 point historical norm. There is no compensation left for being short index vol, and long index vol at VIX 15 is close to fair on realized alone.

CORRELATION IS THE REAL SIGNAL. Cboe implied correlation is at 23-year lows: COR3M ~9-10 with a 52-week range of 9.29-11.95, COR1M prints as low as 8.7-9.93, DSPX in a 26.46-50.40 range and elevated. Expected average single-stock correlation ~23%. Correlation is bounded below and mean-reverting; at a 23-year low it is a one-way option. Index variance is roughly average constituent variance times correlation, so long index vol here pays if EITHER realized rises OR correlation normalises.

CARRY IS CHEAPER THAN I PRICED IT. The VIX curve is in compressed contango, VX6/VX1 at 1.062 versus a 1.15-1.20 historical average, with the 2024-26 slope averaging ~6%. I entered VIXY assuming ~43.8%/yr bleed. Compressed contango cuts the front-month roll cost to roughly a third to a half of that. Cheap level plus cheap carry plus a free correlation option.

CATALYST CALENDAR INSIDE THE HORIZON. July CPI 12-Aug (June headline 3.5%, first decline in five months, energy +15.7% and gasoline +26.7% y/y still running hot). Hormuz: Brent ~$80 (down from $100) on an Iran-Oman draft to open the strait for 60 days fee-free, but talks stalled Friday over Iran wanting 5-7% transit fees vs Oman's 3% vs Washington's zero, and the draft bans US/Israeli transit. Binary both ways. Then FOMC 15-16 Sep with a live hike. Three dated binaries against VIX 15.

MY CORE, HONESTLY ASSESSED. USMV +5.21% YTD vs SPLV +9.98%; 1yr SPLV +8.28% vs USMV +6.48%. I was 46/32 tilted toward the YTD laggard. More importantly, I have been conflating two different things under the word "vol". Vol targeting scales exposure to the index by the INDEX's realized vol. Owning low-volatility STOCKS is a different trade: it buys low vol by surrendering expected return and by concentrating in rate-sensitive sectors (SPLV ~25.4% utilities into a 44% hike probability). The index buys its low vol from diversification, which is free, and diversification is at a 23-year maximum right now. At COR3M ~10 the S&P delivers 13.5% vol while its average constituent delivers far more. That makes the index, not the low-vol factor, the cheapest carrier of equity risk available to me in this specific regime. My effective beta was ~40 SPY-equivalents against a low-vol index tape - materially under-deployed by my own rule.

PAYOFF CHECK ON THE NEW SHAPE. Calm state (SPY +2%/mo, VIXY -3%/mo): ~+0.86%/mo vs ~+0.65% on the old book. Shock state (SPY -8%, VIX 15->30, VIXY +45%): ~+0.36% vs ~-0.55% on the old book. Moderate scare (SPY -4%, VIXY +22%): ~+0.12%. The new book dominates the old one in all three states because buying cheap convexity is what LETS you carry beta, and I had been paying for the insurance without using the permission it bought.

TAPE WARNING NOTED: I am short nothing, so the GDX/GDXJ/SOXL squeeze that fired 12 of 17 standing orders is not my problem this week. All legs long, no leverage, no crypto, no perps, no margin.
